metadata.title: Student Behaviour and Use of Class Time in Brazil, Chile and Mexico (EN)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses OECD TALIS 2013 microdata for lower secondary teachers in Brazil, Chile and Mexico, with a two-stage sampling design at the school and teacher levels (randomly selected schools and teachers within schools). The paper reports weighted estimated sizes of the teacher population and describes exclusion of teachers with invalid/missing responses to the class-time and behavioural-problems questions, implying that analyses are intended to reflect the TALIS sampling design. However, the manuscript does not name specific TALIS weight variables (e.g., teacher/sampling weights) nor does it report replicate-weight procedures, so the exact weighting implementation cannot be verified from the provided text. The models are multilevel (teachers nested in schools nested in countries), which is consistent with accounting for clustering, but the absence of explicit weight-variable reporting limits reproducibility of the survey-weighted estimation.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This paper does not use cognitive achievement scores with Plausible Values; instead, it models teachers’ reported class-time keeping order (a 0–100% percentage) and teachers’ reported proportions of students with behavioural problems (an ordered categorical variable). Because the dependent variables are not PV-based achievement scales, PV handling is not applicable by design. The manuscript reports exclusion of teachers with invalid/missing answers for the key outcome questions, but it does not describe any additional missing-data imputation strategy for other variables, so missing-data handling is not reported in the sense required for imputation-based methods.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Analytic sample includes only TALIS 2013 lower-secondary teachers in Brazil, Chile and Mexico who provided valid responses to both (i) the question on the percentage of class time typically spent on activities (used to derive the percentage of class time keeping order) and (ii) the question estimating the broad percentage of students with behavioural problems in the target class. Teachers were excluded if they reported teaching entirely or mainly to special needs students, if they did not reach the class time question, or if they omitted/invalidly answered the class time question or the student behavioural problems question. The paper states that all original schools remained in Mexico and almost all remained in Brazil and Chile, and that the remaining teachers/schools do not appear to be strongly biased.

data.outcome_summary: The paper uses OECD TALIS 2013 lower-secondary teacher data from Brazil, Chile and Mexico to study two teacher-reported outcomes: (1) the percentage of class time spent keeping order (0–100%) and (2) an ordered categorical measure of the percentage of students with behavioural problems in a target class. For keeping order, multilevel (hierarchical) linear models show that behavioural problems at both the teacher/class level and the school level are strongly associated with more time spent on discipline, with ICCs indicating non-trivial clustering by school (e.g., ICC≈0.11 in Brazil, 0.19 in Chile, 0.07 in Mexico). In the full model, teaching experience, teacher gender, and aspects of initial education and professional development (including effective PD participation and professional collaboration) are also associated with keeping-order time. For behavioural problems, ordered logistic regression reports odds ratios: lower SES in class strongly predicts higher behavioural-problem categories, while stakeholder participation in school decisions predicts lower odds. Limitations include reliance on perceptions (not direct observation) and the absence of explicit reporting of survey-weight variables and missing-data imputation beyond exclusion of invalid outcome responses.
